claim: BE 6/2 40 records Ama-sukkal bringing nineteen shekels into her marriage.
primary_evidence: D01; S01 p. 35, clauses A–B; S03 catalogue
secondary_interpretation: Poebel’s opening translation changes the apparent grammatical agent.
counterevidence_disagreement: Grammatical agency does not establish who chose the partner or where either lived.
generalization_limit: This documented contribution, not every Nippur marriage.
project_relevance: A woman’s transactional role is visible without a household census.

claim: The same contract stipulates repudiation consequences for either spouse, but treats her original silver differently.
primary_evidence: D01; S01 p. 35, clauses C.a–b: return versus forfeiture, plus a half-mina payment
secondary_interpretation: S05 discusses the dossier’s marital interpretation.
counterevidence_disagreement: Parallel clauses are not equal economic consequences or proof that divorce occurred.
generalization_limit: Conditional terms in one contract; no divorce frequency inferred.
project_relevance: Relationship dissolution and property consequences must be distinguished.

claim: BE 6/2 48 stipulates a monetary penalty for the husband but a sale sanction for the wife’s repudiation.
primary_evidence: D04; S01 pp. 36–37, clause C.1; P283604 concordance in S11
secondary_interpretation: S10 places parental/marital sanctions in legal context.
counterevidence_disagreement: The additional bodily-marking/shaving clause is philologically unsettled here; no execution of the sanction demonstrated.
generalization_limit: No universal female divorce penalty; D01 already supplies different terms.
project_relevance: Gender differentiation varies by documented arrangement.

claim: BE 6/2 48 creates a mother–sons relationship between Naramtum and Awiliya’s three sons alongside marriage.
primary_evidence: D04; S01 pp. 35–37, clauses A.2 and C.2; S11 identifies MC 3 16
secondary_interpretation: S10 n. 18 corroborates the relevant Nippur text.
counterevidence_disagreement: Mother/son terminology here is not proof of birth, minority, residence or the previous wife’s death.
generalization_limit: One explicitly constituted relationship, not a general adoption system.
project_relevance: Kinship labels can arise through a legal act rather than descent alone.

claim: In that arrangement, recognition and maintenance of Naramtum are linked to rights in Awiliya’s estate.
primary_evidence: D04; S01 pp. 36–37, clauses C.2–D; provisions for grain, oil and wool
secondary_interpretation: S10 distinguishes sanctions within constituted parenthood.
counterevidence_disagreement: Written future duties do not establish performance or an exclusive provider relationship.
generalization_limit: The specified agreement; no assumption about elderly age.
project_relevance: Support can connect people without demonstrating shared residence.

claim: SAOC 44 34 documents a witnessed marital arrangement; its precise betrothal stage remains interpretive.
primary_evidence: D13; S02 pp. 64, 217; opening discussed in S05 n. 34
secondary_interpretation: Father’s assent and betrothal interpretation in Stone/Greengus.
counterevidence_disagreement: Stone qualifies the interpretation; father identification is queried in the index.
generalization_limit: No universal ceremony, required age, consummation sequence or residential transfer.
project_relevance: Formation may involve kin and witnesses beyond the couple.

claim: The category of the additional payment in BE 6/2 47 is disputed.
period_date: Old Babylonian; exact date not independently checked
primary_evidence: D02; ancient text reached here through S05/S06, not a new edition reading
secondary_interpretation: S06 p. 144 §14 restores terḫatum; S05 interprets an augmented dowry.
counterevidence_disagreement: Reading, restoration and linkage of separate texts matter to the payment label.
generalization_limit: Confidence concerns the documented scholarly disagreement, not which reading wins.
project_relevance: Transfers cannot all be assigned one marriage-payment category.

claim: Scholars disagree about the marital stage dissolved in the BE 6/2 40/47/58 dossier.
period_date: Old Babylonian; BE 40 dated, BE 58 undated here
primary_evidence: D01–D03; S05 manuscript pp. 13–14; S07 pp. 632–634
secondary_interpretation: Greengus argues against an inchoate-marriage reconstruction associated with Westbrook.
counterevidence_disagreement: Westbrook’s book was not independently consulted; dossier chronology is not fully audited.
generalization_limit: Neither interpretation establishes a citywide marriage sequence.
project_relevance: Distinguish evidence of dissolution from assumptions about an earlier stage.

claim: PBS 8/2 116 obliges four brothers/heirs to maintain their sister Bēltani, with inheritance consequences for default.
primary_evidence: D05; S13 tablet obv. 1–12, case parallel; rev. 1–5 concerns alienation
secondary_interpretation: S04 p. 59; exact field owner/reference remains disputed.
counterevidence_disagreement: Future support and field restrictions are not evidence of payments made or co-residence.
generalization_limit: Named parties and stated obligations only.
project_relevance: Sibling duties can persist alongside property and institutional ties.

claim: Unnubtum, identified as a nadītu of Ninurta, appears among witnesses in the same instrument.
primary_evidence: S13 tablet rev. 13; case rev. 11; witness identified as daughter of Ur-baba on case
secondary_interpretation: S07 separately discusses women witnesses in BE 6/2 58.
counterevidence_disagreement: Witnessing does not establish residence with the principals or equal legal capacity in all matters.
generalization_limit: Presence in this record, not a witness participation rate.
project_relevance: Women appear in distinct documentary roles, not only as wives or beneficiaries.

claim: Stone’s account of ARN 29 connects a nadītu woman’s property/support arrangements to several natal relatives.
period_date: Old Babylonian; exact date unverified here
primary_evidence: D06; ARN 29 not directly re-edited here
secondary_interpretation: S04 pp. 57–59 identifies aunt-, father- and brother-related transfers/obligations.
counterevidence_disagreement: Dates and precise clauses need checking in S15; connection with D05 is a scholarly reconstruction.
generalization_limit: No automatic inference of a single joint estate or common dwelling.
project_relevance: Natal ties need not be replaced by one later affiliation.

claim: Stone reports a brother’s intervention in a dispute over Lamasum’s maintenance.
period_date: Old Babylonian; exact date unverified here
primary_evidence: D07; primary text reached through S04
secondary_interpretation: S04 pp. 60–61 describes arrears and a support provider distinct from the brother.
counterevidence_disagreement: Procedural capacity, terms and outcome require primary verification.
generalization_limit: One reported dispute; not universal male guardianship.
project_relevance: Kinship, provision and legal representation need not coincide.

claim: SAOC 44 1 combines marriage with affiliation of the wife’s three children; Stol identifies the wife as a widow.
primary_evidence: D10; S02 p. 215; S11 concordance to MC 3 14
secondary_interpretation: S06 p. 145 n. 67 identifies widowhood/remarriage and brothers as witnesses.
counterevidence_disagreement: Widowhood remains mediated; child ages, prior residence and actual relocation not established.
generalization_limit: Specific relationship reconstitution, not the normal fate of widows.
project_relevance: A marital transition can also alter children’s legal relationships.

claim: SAOC 44 40 is catalogued as litigation about support of a boy(?) by Ipquga(?).
primary_evidence: D15; S02 Appendix IV p. 218 and personal-name index
secondary_interpretation: Catalogue identifies a child-support question; index adds uncertainty.
counterevidence_disagreement: No securely identified guardian, orphan status, age threshold or custody rule.
generalization_limit: Catalogue-level identification; both question marks retained.
project_relevance: Children’s needs are visible without inventing a complete guardianship system.

claim: The SAOC 44 44/46/47 sequence records joint property acquisition followed by one partner’s share purchase.
primary_evidence: D16–D18; S02 Appendix IV p. 218
secondary_interpretation: S02 pp. 65–68 identifies the partners as brothers and relates documents to houses.
counterevidence_disagreement: Legal shares do not prove former or later co-residence; architectural allocations remain reconstructed.
generalization_limit: These property acts, not a documented census-level household split.
project_relevance: Property division is relevant to, but not identical with, residential separation.

claim: SAOC 44 25 associates Asirum’s residence with a house whose purchase involved several contributors.
primary_evidence: D11; S02 pp. 63, 217 and index s.v. Asirum
secondary_interpretation: Stone proposes an occupancy-preservation reading; a debt arrangement is an alternative.
counterevidence_disagreement: Number of contributors differs internally; their full kin relations and residence are unproved.
generalization_limit: Asirum’s reported residence does not make every contributor an occupant.
project_relevance: Co-residence, financing, ownership and kinship must be assessed separately.

claim: SAOC 44 31 preserves an inherited house interest outside Nippur in a Nippur find context.
primary_evidence: D12; S02 Appendix IV p. 217
secondary_interpretation: S02 p. 63 discusses wider affiliations of this assemblage.
counterevidence_disagreement: A distant asset does not demonstrate migration, ethnicity or a household’s relocation.
generalization_limit: Specified property connection only.
project_relevance: Legal associations can extend beyond the site where documents survive.

claim: SAOC 44 50 records a time-limited house rental rather than an ownership transfer.
primary_evidence: D19; S02 Appendix IV p. 218
secondary_interpretation: No additional residential reconstruction adopted.
counterevidence_disagreement: Contracted access is not proof of actual occupancy or all occupants’ identities.
generalization_limit: One rental; tenant household size and kin composition unknown.
project_relevance: Residence-related access need not entail ownership.

claim: SAOC 44 53 records manumission, but its catalogue does not establish a residential departure.
primary_evidence: D20; S02 Appendix IV p. 218
secondary_interpretation: No broader dependency classification imported.
counterevidence_disagreement: Freedom/status change is not automatically exit from a dwelling or all prior ties.
generalization_limit: Recorded legal act; post-release residence and service unknown.
project_relevance: Legal status transitions and household association can diverge.

claim: The examined Nippur evidence does not establish a universal nadītu residence or reproductive regime.
primary_evidence: D05; D08–D09 are cautionary leads, not newly collated counterexamples
secondary_interpretation: S04 p. 56 discusses residential terminology, identity and parenthood ambiguities.
counterevidence_disagreement: Male ownership near nadītu housing does not prove male occupancy; a son label need not mean biological birth.
generalization_limit: This is a limit of the examined evidence, not proof that no restrictions existed.
project_relevance: A religious designation cannot alone determine all personal relationships.

claim: Stone’s proposed close-kin marriage pattern rests on sparse reconstructed cases.
primary_evidence: No representative marriage sample established; see D21 for one reconstructed network
secondary_interpretation: S02 pp. 15–19 advances an endogamy interpretation with limited examples.
counterevidence_disagreement: Adoptive and biological relatedness must not be collapsed; no frequency denominator.
generalization_limit: Evidence does not establish routine citywide cousin marriage.
project_relevance: Observed or reconstructed kin links must not become demographic defaults.

claim: A recent Ur-Pabilsaĝa reconstruction links marriage, adoption and transactions across more than one family grouping.
primary_evidence: D21; component records not all reread in this project
secondary_interpretation: S14 pp. 1–4, fig. 1; Alī-aḫātī’s remarriage is part of the reconstruction.
counterevidence_disagreement: Chronological reorderings are contested; figure labels are modern analytical groupings.
generalization_limit: Not a complete genealogy, household census or independent replication of every link.
project_relevance: People can participate in several family relationships simultaneously.

claim: The find context of SAOC 44 1 is a foundation context, not a directly observed occupancy roster.
primary_evidence: D10; S02 Appendix IV p. 215
secondary_interpretation: Present report draws a source-critical inference from the catalogue context.
counterevidence_disagreement: The precise deposition process was not independently reconstructed.
generalization_limit: A foundation find alone cannot identify its depositors as the contract’s household.
project_relevance: Document provenance and lived residence are different evidentiary questions.
